book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

chapters.relation: Steven Neumann reads the sold-my-soul legends around Led Zeppelin ('here's to my sweet Satan' backwards on 'Stairway to Heaven'), Black Sabbath, and bluesman Robert Johnson at the Clarksdale crossroads as a parable of Nietzsche's amor fati: every joy comes bundled with suffering, so greatness means affirming the whole package. He deploys the eternal recurrence thought experiment - would you will your life, Plant's dead son and Bonham's fatal bender included, to repeat eternally? - and contrasts the ascetic denial of pleasure with Nietzsche's claim in Ecce Homo that his own sickness and obscurity made him love fate all the more.

Nick Jones asks whether worshipping the Devil and doing evil can ever be good, and answers: artistically yes. Using the transgression that defines extreme metal - blasphemy, church burnings, and Varg Vikernes's murder of Euronymous - he argues Satanic metal's immoral features can enhance its artistic value when they achieve three aims: rebellion, blasphemy, and authenticity. Genuine theistic Satanists who really believe in the Devil they invoke do all three best, though the chapter ends by conceding the cupboard of actual theistic Satanist metalheads is empty.

Liz Stillwaggon Swan explains why crime dramas like Criminal Minds, CSI, and Bones are so watchable: Jung's shadow archetype and collective unconscious mean the Devil in human form on screen taps humanity's shared dark layer, while Aristotle's catharsis lets viewers experience pity and fear safely from the couch, identifying with characters like repulsed Garcia or intellectualizing Dr. Brennan. She adds the CSI effect - jurors with warped expectations of DNA and fingerprint work - and argues the shows satisfy a deep need to see devils like Bundy and Dahmer caught within a tidy forty-three minutes.

Jeff Ewing reads Faustian bargains - Marlowe's and Goethe's Faust, Dorian Gray's wager with Lord Henry, Tommy Johnson's guitar in O Brother Where Art Thou?, Rosemary's Baby, and Twilight Zone's 'Escape Clause' - through Marx's Capital. The soul becomes a universal commodity with both use value and exchange value, and the Devil a perfect buyer's monopoly who can demand everything, a trade Ewing contrasts with capitalism's effective-demand rule that those who cannot pay go unaided even unto death.

Roger Hunt reads Bill Hicks's stand-up as a Socratic comedy exposing Satan's three-point plan: suppress knowledge, breed ignorance, and profit from hypocrisy - from the Waffle House 'readah' scene to Bush-era Gulf War spin ('we looked at the receipts'), JFK-assassination distraction via American Gladiators, and pop stars and marketers who 'suck Satan's cock' (Rick Astley, corporate rock, advertising). Where the Genesis serpent offered knowledge, Hicks's Devil is the force that suppresses it, and Hicks paid a Socratic price - an early death for 'corrupting' his audience - for pointing this out.

Jones, Hansmann, and Stachura trace the trope of woman as the Devil's handmaiden - Eve and Lilith, succubae and Sirens, the sixteenth-century witch hunts, down to 'maneater' and 'Poison' rock songs and Blurred Lines - arguing it perpetuates patriarchal power. They apply Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman constructed as the perpetual Other, defined as secondary to man with sexuality at the heart of her Othering, and extend the analysis with Gloria Anzaldua's Borderlands and mestiza consciousness, which rejects the gender binary the woman-as-Devil trope depends on.

Aaron Rabinowitz argues that modern Devil stories - Milton's 'Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven', Neil Gaiman's Sandman where Lucifer quits Hell like a two-weeks notice, and Mike Carey's Lucifer building a second creation whose only commandment forbids worship - reveal a Devil whose real motive is free will and autonomy in a predetermined cosmos. Rereading the serpent in Eden, the wager over Job, and the temptation of Jesus through that lens makes Lucifer look reasonable, even commendable, and since we all feel pushed around by obligations, survival needs, and neuroscience, our sympathy for the Devil is inevitable.

Tim Jones tests Kundera's thesis that the Devil stands for meaninglessness against the angels' excess of imposed meaning. The Quran's Iblis refuses to bow to Adam but really just wants his own hierarchy with himself on top; the Devil's temptations of Jesus in the desert (stones into bread, the temple leap, dominion in exchange for worship) pick apart the meaning of Jesus's fast only to install his own significance; and Lord of the Flies shows how the conch's collapse into 'just a glorified seashell' lets Jack's hunters turn the island into Hell - so the grinning, meaning-destroying Devil of the pig's head is as terrifying as a plainly evil one.

James Edwin Mahon dismantles the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle by testing three accounts of diabolical evil: Machiavelli's prince ('learn how not to be virtuous') shows self-interest is mere amoral Realpolitik; Schopenhauer's malice and Schadenfreude ('injure all people as far as you can') are still self-interested pleasure; and only Kant's 'diabolical will' - doing evil because it is evil, Paradise Lost's 'Evil, be thou my good' - truly captures the Devil, though Kant deemed it impossible for humans. Hence nobody actually likes the Devil; people like the intelligence, charm, and underdog status of the characters who play him in The Devil's Advocate and Angel Heart.

Greg Littmann asks whether the Devil could actually get you by testing theories of the afterlife against Hamlet's ghost, Freddy Krueger, the possessions of The Exorcist and Evil Dead, Paranormal Activity, Dante's Inferno, Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, and Doom. Substance dualism cannot explain how a non-physical soul moves so much as a finger; the view that you are your body founders on recycled grave matter and the primacy of the brain; and if you are a program running on your brain, the Devil could torture infinite copies of you in Hell - even re-running you there from Heaven - unless duplication means neither copy is really you.

John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.

Robert Arp treats Voltaire's 'If God did not exist, then it would be necessary to invent Him' as a conditional claim and argues it is false: Kant's categorical imperative (universalize the action, as with lying and the collapsing practice of borrowing) and Mill's utilitarian cost-benefit calculus secure social order with no god and no Devil required. He then concedes that since most people are driven by guilt and fear rather than reason, inventing the Devil as an archetype of evil to be avoided at all costs may after all be a useful fiction.

Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.

Clint Jones argues LaVey's Satanic Bible rests on a misreading of Epicurus: genuine Epicurean hedonism is not limitless indulgence but the ordered life of the Tetrapharmakon - don't fear gods or death, the good is easy to get, pain is endurable - together with the threefold division of desires, which reserves constant gratification for natural and necessary things like water, bread, and friendship. By licensing gluttony and every whim so long as no one else is hurt, LaVeyan Satanism fails as the pleasure-as-virtue philosophy it claims to revive, leaving its followers with base, unfulfilling pleasures that are, well, Hellish.

Magus Peter Gilmore, High Priest of the Church of Satan, reads pop culture's turn to villains - Loki outshining Thor, Ledger's Joker, Hellboy, Man of Steel's killing Superman - as the mainstream finally arriving at the Satanist party, since LaVeyans always used Satan as a symbol of self-deification ('I-theist') and carnal pride. He answers Pitkänen that Satanism needs no 'higher knowledge' and cannot include theists, and he answers Jones by citing the Satanic Bible chapter 'INDULGENCE... NOT COMPULSION': LaVey taught self-controlled indulgence and rational self-interest, not reckless abandon, and Epicurean moderation is no basis for dismissing him.

Olli Pitkanen replies to Magus Peter Gilmore's critique: against the Church of Satan's claim to own 'Satanism', he argues definitions are never stable (materialism means Democritus', Newton's, quantum or Marx's) and that had LaVey's church never formed in the 1960s, some other - probably more religious - Satanism would have defined the term differently, so no group has final authority over the label.

Clint Jones answers Magus Gilmore by conceding he judged only The Satanic Bible but arguing that is the right target: even if LaVey later refined his views, he never retracted the book's Epicurean pretensions, and naming his system Epicurean is itself an appeal to an intellectual forebear. Since LaVey 'plundered' his sources - cherry-picking 'pretty gemstones rather than weightier keystones' - the foundation of Satanism remains shaky, and a Garden of Eden stripped of its Judeo-Christian trappings, Jones adds, was already a remarkably Epicurean life.

Magus Peter Gilmore closes the exchange: LaVeyan Satanism honestly embraces the selfishness most people already live by (sharing Ayn Rand's enshrined self-interest), and Epicurus's own letters to Menoeceus - on not fearing death, choosing the most pleasant over the longest life, pragmatic justice, and the need for natural science - show deep congruence with LaVey. Against Pitkänen on Eastern religions, whose reincarnation and karmic debt he reads as denigration of carnal existence, and against Jones's shaky-foundation charge (Christianity itself was a Hebraic/Hellenic mash-up), he concludes Satanists are proud 'Hell-raisers' celebrating the only life there is.

Robert Arp compiles the 'Devil made me do it' record: Flip Wilson's catchphrase, actual possession pleas from Christian v. State to the Demon Murder Trial of Arne Cheyenne Johnson, the M'Naghten Rule born of Daniel M'Naghten's botched assassination, the Son of Sam's possessed dog Harvey, exorcism lore from Roland Doe (The Exorcist) to Anneliese Michel (The Exorcism of Emily Rose), and the bizarre Mayo v. Satan lawsuit. The law's answer throughout is that only a defect of reason - never the Devil - robs defendants of free will, and the possession cases read better as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and negligence than as demons.

holes.name: Immoralism in Aesthetics (moralism vs autonomism vs immoralism)
holes.what: The aesthetics debate over whether an artwork's immoral features count against, are irrelevant to, or can actually improve its artistic value.
holes.why: Chapter 46's whole argument is that Satanic metal's immorality (blasphemy, church burnings) can enhance its artistic value, a position taxonomy has no slug for.

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation through tragedy)
holes.what: Aristotle's idea that watching tragedy lets an audience safely experience pity and fear and so purges those emotions.
holes.why: Chapter 48 uses catharsis as its second pillar for explaining why TV crime dramas like Criminal Minds and CSI entertain millions while feeling psychologically healthy.

holes.name: Labor Theory of Value (use value and exchange value)
holes.what: Marx's Capital analysis that commodities have use value and labor-grounded exchange value, the basis of exploitation, prices, and monopoly power.
holes.why: Chapter 49's entire reading of the Faustian bargain treats the soul as a universal commodity with use and exchange value sold to a monopolist Devil, a framework taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Gloria Anzaldúa
holes.what: Chicana feminist theorist of the Borderlands who exposes binary identity as an oversimplification of lived experience and advocates a mestiza consciousness embracing ambiguity.
holes.why: Chapter 52 extends Beauvoir's Othering analysis of the woman-as-Devil trope with Anzaldúa's Borderlands and her critique of the gender dichotomy, but taxonomy has no entry for her.

holes.name: Milan Kundera
holes.what: Novelist-essayist whose The Book of Laughter and Forgetting casts the Devil as meaninglessness set against the angels' excess of imposed meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 56 adopts Kundera's Devil-as-meaninglessness thesis as its entire framework and tests it against Iblis, the temptation of Jesus, and Lord of the Flies.

holes.name: The Diabolical Will
holes.what: Kant's notion of a will that does evil precisely because it is evil, which he held impossible for humans and proper to the Devil alone.
holes.why: Chapter 57's conclusion is that neither Machiavellian self-interest nor Schopenhauerian malice captures the Devil, whose evil requires Kant's diabolical will.

holes.name: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)
holes.what: French Enlightenment deist and satirist, author of Candide's attack on Leibnizian optimism and the quip that if God did not exist it would be necessary to invent Him.
holes.why: Chapter 62 is built entirely around evaluating Voltaire's claim that God and the Devil are socially necessary inventions, and taxonomy lacks any entry for him.

holes.name: Anton Szandor LaVey
holes.what: Founder of the Church of Satan (1966) whose Satanic Bible frames atheistic Satanism as carnal self-deification, self-controlled indulgence, and rational self-interest.
holes.why: Chapters 65, 69, 70, 72, and 73 debate LaVey's Satanism directly - its hedonism, its definition, its Epicurean debts - yet taxonomy has no slug for the philosopher at their center.
